display_title: I Keep My Hands Outside My Pants in Public
audience: non-verbal and minimally speaking teens with autism, AAC users, life-skills classes
tone: respectful, clear, age-neutral, non-shaming, not babyish
real_world_context: Body Safety & Boundaries — private touching / masturbation in public
demand_signal: High: TPT has specific private parts/touching-public social stories but none with AAC, lanyards, routine strips, choice boards, or data sheets. Major differentiation gap.
design_philosophy: TOOLKIT WITH OPTIONS — not prescriptions. Teachers select which pages, cards, and strips are appropriate for their specific student and context. Every replacement behavior has multiple options because one-answer products fail real students (e.g. telling a student 'do it at home' created a new problem of wanting to go home).
story_pages: Some parts of my body are private parts.
Private parts are the parts I cover with my underwear or my swimsuit.
It is okay to touch my own private parts. This is normal.
But I can only touch my private parts in a private place.
Public means other people can see me, like in the classroom, hallway, playground, bus or shops.
Private means I am alone with the door closed, like my bedroom at home.
At school and in the community, I keep my hands outside my pants.
If I want to touch my private parts in public, I wait.
I can keep my hands busy instead. I can hold a fidget, put my hands on my desk, or squeeze my hands together.
If I need to fix my clothes, I can go to the bathroom.
If I am unsure, I can ask a safe adult.
I can use words, pictures or AAC to say 'I need help' or 'I need a break.'
No one else should touch my private parts. I can say 'no' and tell a safe adult.
If I forget the rule, that is okay. I can try again next time.
Keeping my hands outside my pants in public helps me stay safe and respectful.
story_teacher_note: The social story uses 'my bedroom at home' as the example private place. This is the safest default because it is clearly home-only and does not risk generalizing to public restrooms (TACA guidance). However, some families and schools choose bathroom instead. If your team chooses bathroom, modify page 5 to say 'my bedroom or the bathroom at home with the door closed' and add explicit discrimination training about WHICH bathrooms are okay. The story is a starting point — adapt it to your student's context.

school: At school, my hands stay outside my pants in class, in the hallway, and at lunch.
If I feel uncomfortable at school, I can ask for a break or use a fidget.
My teacher can help me remember.
Private body care is for home — in the private place my family chooses.
home: At home, I have a private place for private body care — with the door closed.
My family will show me which place is my private place.
At home, I can ask a trusted adult if I need help or have questions.
I wash my hands when I am finished.
community: In the community — shops, bus, park — my hands stay outside my pants.
Private body care is for home, not for public places.
If I feel uncomfortable, I can use a fidget or ask for a break.
story_optional_context_pages.note_for_teachers: Print only the context pages relevant to your student. The home page deliberately says 'my family will show me which place is my private place' rather than naming a specific room — because different families choose different places (bedroom, bathroom, or both). Adapt the home page to name the specific place your student's family has chosen. See the alternative behavior options sheet for considerations about bedroom vs bathroom.

mini_book.title: My Hands Stay Outside My Pants
mini_book.source: Same content as story_pages — smaller print size for portability.
mini_book.print_format: Print at reduced size, cut, staple, or hole-punch for a ring. Fits in a bag or pocket. Student can carry between settings (school to home).
mini_book.note: No separate content — uses the same story_pages as the social story, just rendered at a smaller page size.

picture_main.description: Large image fills 50-65% of the page. Short text at top — one sentence per page. Matches published Small Wins Studio format (Private Parts are Private, How to Change a Pad). Best for non-verbal students and visual learners who need the image to carry the meaning.

text_main.description: Smaller image (30-40% of page) with more text room. Same story_pages content but allows for longer sentences or additional context. Best for students who read or are learning to read, and for teacher reference.

story_layout_versions.note_for_teachers: TWO layout versions are provided. Print the one that suits your student. Picture-main matches the published Small Wins Studio format — the image carries the meaning and the text is a single short sentence. Text-main has a smaller image with more room for text — use this for students who read or for your own reference. Both versions use the SAME story content.

cut_out_pieces.title: Cut-Out Pieces
cut_out_pieces.description: ONE set of cut-out pieces used across multiple components: lanyards, participation matching, and routine strips. Teacher prints and cuts the pieces, then deploys them as needed. Includes both bedroom and bathroom pieces so the teacher can select based on their student's plan.

deployment.participation: Use all pieces. Student matches each cut-out to the correct social story page during or after reading. For non-verbal students: teacher reads the page, student finds and places the matching piece.
deployment.routine_strip: Select 3-5 pieces. Teacher places them on the standard routine strip template to build a location-specific routine.

cut_out_pieces.note_for_teachers: Print one sheet of cut-out pieces. Cut them up. Use the SAME pieces for story matching and routine strips. Not every student needs every piece — select what works for your student. Both 'My bedroom' and 'Bathroom' pieces are included so you can select based on your student's plan. If you use the bathroom piece, pair it with explicit discrimination training about WHICH bathrooms are okay. See the alternative behavior options sheet for considerations. NOTE: For lanyard use, see the Visual Support Cards product — it uses the same card content in a small lanyard format.

routine_strip_template.title: Routine Strip Template
routine_strip_template.description: Standard blank template with the format: '___ behaviour is for ___ location/time'. Teacher selects cut-out pieces and places them on the template to build a location-specific routine. Different students and families will choose different private places — build the routine that matches your student's plan.

routine_strip_template.note_for_teachers: Print the blank template. Select the cut-out pieces that match your student's context and routine. Place them on the template. Laminate. Not every student needs the same routine — build what works for THIS student in THIS setting. Both bedroom and bathroom examples are included — choose the one that matches your student's plan. If you use bathroom, pair it with explicit discrimination training about WHICH bathrooms are okay.

alternative_behavior_options.title: Alternative Behavior Options — Teacher Selection Sheet
alternative_behavior_options.description: A generic page of alternative behavior icons. Teacher selects which options are appropriate for their student, behavior, or phase. This is a SELECTION sheet, not a prescription. Different students, families, and schools will choose different options based on their context, values, and the function of the behavior.
research_basis: Matched stimulation: provide sensory items that meet the same sensory need (Piazza et al., 1998)
RIRD: redirect to physical activities using both hands — moving chairs, touching toes (research-proven for public masturbation)
Functional communication training: teach requesting break/help via AAC (Davis et al., 2015)
Deep pressure: weighted vest, compression clothing, lap pad — for body sensory input
Movement breaks: walking laps, trampoline, climbing — for proprioceptive seekers
Discrimination training: teach public vs private (Vanderbilt Kennedy Center, CSESA, ASERT)
Function-based: replacement must match WHY the behavior occurs (ASAT, Autism NZ)
Non-shaming: don't label behavior as 'bad' — teach WHERE not just 'stop' (TACA, Vanderbilt, Autism Speaks)

options.function: Escape from sensory overload or task demand
Hands busy with sensory item — matched stimulation
Drawing, putty, Lego, zip board — both hands occupied

options.text: Press my feet to the floor
Use my bedroom at home (door closed)
options.function: Private place at home for private body care
options.considerations: TACA recommends bedroom as the private place because it is clearly home-only and does not risk generalizing to public restrooms. Some families and practitioners prefer this approach.

options.text: Use the bathroom at home (door closed)
options.function: Private place at home for private body care — some families prefer bathroom
options.considerations: Some families and practitioners use the bathroom at home successfully. TACA warns this can generalize to ALL bathrooms including public restrooms — if you choose this option, pair it with explicit discrimination training about WHICH bathrooms are okay (home bathroom only, not school or public).

options.text: Use the bathroom at school (door closed)
options.function: Private place at school — some schools permit this
options.considerations: Some schools and practitioners use the school bathroom as a private place. TACA warns about generalization risk. If you choose this option, pair it with explicit discrimination training: THIS bathroom at school, not ALL bathrooms. Discuss with your school team and BCBA.

options.function: Visual timer — 'private time in 30 minutes' — for teens who need to know when they can have privacy

alternative_behavior_options.note_for_teachers: This is a SELECTION sheet, not a prescription. Different students, families, and schools will choose different options. Print the page. Cut out the options that work for YOUR student in YOUR setting and YOUR values. Laminate and add Velcro to the choice board. Not every option is available in every classroom or home. Not every option works for every student. The FUNCTION of the behavior determines which replacement will work — if the behavior is sensory-seeking, try fidget/compression/movement. If it's escape, try break/help. If it's automatic reinforcement, try matched stimulation. Consult your BCBA or OT for individualized recommendations. IMPORTANT NOTES: (1) The bedroom vs bathroom decision is a family/school choice — both options are included. TACA recommends bedroom to avoid generalization to public restrooms. Some practitioners use bathroom successfully with explicit discrimination training. We present both options and let you decide. (2) Whatever private place you choose, pair it with explicit teaching about WHICH specific places are okay — do not assume the student will generalize correctly. (3) Check medical causes (yeast, histamine) if behavior is new or suddenly increased — consult a doctor. (4) Never shame or punish — this can make the behavior worse and drive it underground.

aac_board.title: My Body Communication Board
aac_board.structure: 6x6 grid — 24 fixed core words (rows 1,2,5,6) + 12 topic-specific fringe words (rows 3,4). Core words are canonical from core_profile.json and never change. Only the fringe words change per topic.
aac_board.note: Uses the BoardReady 6x6 structure with canonical core words. Only the 12 fringe words (rows 3-4) are topic-specific. Board is for non-verbal and minimally speaking students to communicate about this topic. 'touch' and 'safe' replace 'uncomfortable' and 'wash_hands' because they are more concrete and essential for this topic — 'uncomfortable' can be communicated with core words ('body' + 'dont_like') and 'wash_hands' with ('go' + 'bathroom'). Both 'bedroom' and 'bathroom' are included so the student can communicate about whichever private place their family has chosen. 'I feel safe' and 'I dont feel safe' added for body safety communication. Autism New Zealand recommends adding 'penis/vagina', 'naked', 'clothes on/clothes off' to the student's full AAC system — these are not on this topic board but should be added to the student's personal device.

scenario_sort.title: Public or Private? — Where Does This Happen?
scenario_sort.description: Students sort scenarios into PUBLIC or PRIVATE. Teaches discrimination — WHERE the behavior is appropriate. TWO versions are provided: a simple 2-mat version with clear boundaries, and an advanced 3-mat version with IT DEPENDS for students who can handle nuance. Teacher selects the version appropriate for their student.

version_simple.description: 2 sorting mats: PUBLIC and PRIVATE. Clear boundaries, no ambiguity. For students who need clear rules. The teacher pre-selects the private place based on the student's plan, so all bathroom scenarios are sorted based on that decision.

scenarios.scenario: I am in the classroom.
I am on the school bus.
I am in my bedroom at home with the door closed.
I am at lunch in the cafeteria.
I am in the hallway between classes.
I am in a shop with my family.
I am at recess on the playground.
I am in a public bathroom at the shops.
I am in a changing room at the pool.
Someone else tries to touch my private parts.
scenarios.note: This is never okay — tell an adult right away. My body belongs to me.

version_simple.note_for_teachers: This version has clear PUBLIC and PRIVATE categories only — no ambiguity. The private place scenarios only include bedroom (the safest default). A body safety scenario about someone ELSE touching is included as PUBLIC (never okay) — this is a clear boundary, not context-dependent. If your student's plan includes bathroom as a private place, add a bathroom card to the PRIVATE mat manually and ensure your student has explicit discrimination training about WHICH bathrooms are private. Remove any scenarios that are not relevant to your student's context.

version_advanced.description: 3 sorting mats: PUBLIC, PRIVATE, and IT DEPENDS. For students who can handle discussion about context and different family/school choices. The IT DEPENDS mat is for scenarios where the answer depends on the family's or school's plan.

Use the IT DEPENDS cards to discuss why different families and schools make different choices. The body safety scenario about someone ELSE touching is PUBLIC (never okay) — this is a clear boundary, not context-dependent. If the student finds IT DEPENDS too confusing, switch to the simple version.

scenario_sort.note_for_teachers: TWO versions are provided. Start with the simple version (PUBLIC/PRIVATE only) for students who need clear boundaries. Move to the advanced version (PUBLIC/PRIVATE/IT DEPENDS) only if the student can handle discussion about context and different choices. Many non-verbal students need the clear boundaries of the simple version — do not assume the advanced version is better.

Teacher selects the version appropriate for their student. Based on Vanderbilt Kennedy Center and ASERT public/private behavior guidance.

reward_chart.title: I Am Working For ___ — Token Board
reward_chart.description: Token board / reward chart for reinforcing use of replacement behaviors. Same format as existing 'I am working for XMAS' product. Teacher selects the reward and the behavior being reinforced.
reward_chart.format: I am working for [REWARD]. I earn a token when I [BEHAVIOR]. When I get [N] tokens, I get my reward.
reward_chart.template: Standard 'I am working for ___' template with blank token spaces. Teacher writes or places a picture of the reward. Student earns tokens for using replacement behaviors.
behaviors_to_reinforce: Used a replacement strategy instead of touching in public
Asked for a break when uncomfortable
Used a fidget or hands-busy activity
Kept hands outside pants in class
Used AAC or pictures to communicate about body or feelings
Told an adult about feeling uncomfortable or unsafe
Went to a private place without being told
Said 'no' or told an adult when someone touched them inappropriately
reward_chart.note_for_teachers: Print the token board. Write or place a picture of the student's preferred reward. Select the behavior being reinforced — not all behaviors at once. Start with one behavior and a low token count (3). Increase as the student becomes consistent. This is the same format as the 'I am working for' charts you may already use.

iep_data_sheet.title: IEP Goals & Data Collection — Private Touching / Public Behavior

goals.goal: Given a visual prompt (lanyard card or routine strip), STUDENT will keep hands outside pants in public settings (classroom, hallway, cafeteria) for ___ consecutive minutes with ___ prompts in a ___ minute observation period.
goals.measurement: Frequency count of incidents + prompt level (independent, verbal, visual, physical)
goals.target: ___ incidents or fewer per ___ minute observation

goals.goal: Given the alternative behavior options sheet, STUDENT will select an appropriate replacement behavior (break, fidget, hands-busy, squeeze hands) when prompted during an uncomfortable body sensation, in ___ of ___ opportunities.
goals.measurement: Opportunity-based: number of correct selections / total opportunities

goals.goal: Given a public/private scenario card, STUDENT will correctly sort the scenario as public or private with ___ accuracy across ___ consecutive sessions.
STUDENT will independently request a break or help using AAC, words, or pictures when experiencing body discomfort in a public setting, in ___ of ___ opportunities.
goals.measurement: Opportunity-based: independent requests / total discomfort episodes

goals.goal: Given a body safety scenario (someone else touching), STUDENT will indicate 'no' or tell an adult using AAC, words, or pictures in ___ of ___ opportunities.
goals.measurement: Opportunity-based: correct safety response / total safety scenarios presented

content_warning: This product addresses private touching / masturbation in public settings for non-verbal and minimally speaking teens with autism. Content is dignity-centered, non-shaming, and teaches WHERE behaviors are appropriate rather than prohibiting them entirely. All content must be reviewed by a classroom practitioner before publishing.

research_sources.source: Vanderbilt Kennedy Center — Healthy Bodies Toolkit
research_sources.key_guidance: Don't shame/punish. Teach WHERE. Use visuals. Set ground rules. Use social narratives. Start early. Use correct anatomical terms.

research_sources.source: Vanderbilt Kennedy Center — Navigating Puberty, Sex & Sexuality
research_sources.key_guidance: Autistic people have inherent sexual rights. Use visuals and real-world experiences. Provide private location rather than only saying stop.

Don't label as 'bad' — drives behavior underground. Teach bedroom (NOT bathroom) as private place to avoid generalization to public restrooms. Check medical causes (yeast, histamine). Consult OT/BCBA.

research_sources.source: ASERT (PA) — Be Safe: Public and Private Places Social Story
research_sources.key_guidance: Public vs private behavior social stories in visual format. Public = eating, talking, hugging. Private = adjusting underwear, touching private parts.
Social stories + visual resources for abuse prevention and body safety. Focus on who can/can't touch, how to say no, how to ask for help.

research_sources.source: Autism New Zealand — Inappropriate Sexual Behaviour
research_sources.key_guidance: Use correct anatomical terms. Add AAC words (penis/vagina, naked, clothes on/off). Use neutral colors NOT red for private parts. Frame as rules/politeness, not shame. List every private space explicitly.

research_sources.source: Autism Speaks — ATN/AIR-P Puberty and Adolescence Resource
research_sources.key_guidance: For less verbal children: adjust language and add visual supports. Masturbation is normal — issue is when/where. Visual supports toolkit available.

research_sources.source: CSESA — Puberty for Adolescents with ASD
research_sources.key_guidance: Teach public/private behaviors. Students may not understand context-dependent rules. Use visual and concrete examples. Reduces bullying and abuse risk.
The desire is not wrong — issue is when/where. Shape behavior, don't suppress. Highly individualized. Assess what individual is interested in and teach safe/appropriate ways.

research_sources.source: Academic — Systematic Review of Interventions for Inappropriate Masturbation (ASD/DD)
research_sources.key_guidance: RIRD and RI both effective. Function-based intervention recommended. Reinforcement-based before punishment-based.

research_sources.source: Academic — Reducing Public Masturbation (RIRD vs RI)
research_sources.key_guidance: RIRD: redirect to physical activities using both hands. RI: interrupt with verbal/physical prompts. Both effective, RI requires fewer resources.
Matched stimulation produces statistically significant decrease in automatically maintained challenging behavior. Provide sensory items meeting the same need.

research_sources.source: Sex Ed Rescue — Replacement Behaviour for Inappropriate Touching
research_sources.key_guidance: Saying 'stop' often doesn't work because behavior meets a need. Identify function first. Supports: fidgets, compression, movement breaks, visual reminders, hands-busy, body boundary teaching, scheduled private time.
